You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

description: Solve ARC grids with rectangular frames and enclosed regions, or noisy solid rectangular fields; infer fills and colors from demonstrations.

# Infer rectangular-region transformations

1. Compare each demonstration's input and output cell by cell. Identify backgrounds, rectangular boundaries, enclosed interiors, and anomalous pixels; classify which spatial structures actually change. A frame around an empty region and a solid noisy rectangle are different branches—do not treat every unusual color as noise or every hollow rectangle as a field to fill.
2. Infer the operation and its scope from demonstrated changes, including which colors and locations qualify. For noisy solid fields, determine from changed and unchanged controls whether anomalies are replaced only inside fields, removed outside, or treated differently; do not assume one blanket rule. Verify the candidate against every demonstrated change and invariant. If distinct rules remain plausible, request another demonstration rather than guessing.
3. Apply only the verified rule to the test. Preserve unrelated objects and background; check bounds, dimensions, and every changed cell against the rule before submitting. Do not submit a speculative interpretation when the demo does not establish it.

# Infer divider-panel outputs

1. In every demonstration, locate the solid divider and measure the panels. Compare output dimensions and cell patterns against each panel (including rotations/reflections only when evidence supports them); determine whether output copies one panel, transforms it, or compares corresponding cells. Do not assume the lower or first panel is selected from orientation alone.
2. Derive the mapping and any cross-panel rule cell by cell from demonstrations. Test every output cell, including cases where candidate inputs differ; reject any rule that misses even one location. Distinguish the candidate's exact condition (for example, a particular color pairing) from merely being in a panel, and track row/column offsets, crop, orientation, and panel dimensions explicitly. If more than one rule fits or none fits, request another demo rather than guessing.
3. Apply only the fully verified rule to the test. Construct the exact demonstrated output dimensions and cell values; independently check each qualifying and nonqualifying position and the separator exclusion before submitting.
